output:
A battery does not hold electricity the way a bucket holds water. It holds a chemical arrangement that is desperate to rearrange itself.

Inside are two different materials, kept apart. One of them holds electrons loosely and would happily give them away. The other would happily accept them. Between the two sits a paste or liquid called the electrolyte. It lets charged particles drift across, but it blocks electrons completely.

That blockage is the whole trick. The electrons cannot take the short route, so they wait. Connect a torch or a phone, and you hand them a longer path around the outside. They rush through your device on the way, and that flow is the current doing work.

Think of water held behind a dam on a hillside. Nothing happens while the wall holds. Open a channel through a mill wheel, and the water goes where it wanted to go anyway, turning the wheel as it passes.

The battery goes flat when the two materials have finished swapping. A rechargeable one lets you push the reaction backwards with mains power, hauling the water back uphill. Eventually the materials degrade and stop cooperating.

In short, a battery stores energy as chemistry under tension, and your device releases it.
